First, what a stuck state is

A stuck state is your nervous system holding onto a protective pattern past the moment it was needed. Your body has built-in responses to threat: speeding up, shutting down, or even holding both at once. They’re supposed to switch on when needed, do their job, and switch off when they’re able to. But what happens when one’s life never allows the switch to turn off?

Two things to know before you read on. First, states are not identities or personalities. These are temporary states of the body, even if it’s been decades. Second, you can be in more than one state, states shift, and have varying intensities.

What sounds familiar?

This isn’t a quiz. There’s no score, no result, and nothing here will tell you what you are (only you can recognize that). This is a list of common experiences. The stuck states, in their own words

Read them as voices, not labels. Notice which one sounds like the inside of your head.

Shutdown

“I’m here, but I’m not really here. People talk to me and I nod, but it’s like the volume on everything got turned down, including me. I used to care about things. I can’t find that anymore.”

Read more about shutdown

Freeze

“I’m screaming on the inside and motionless on the outside. I want to do the thing, I think about doing the thing constantly, and I cannot make my body start. It’s not laziness. It’s like slamming the gas and the brake at the same time.”

Read more about freeze

Flight

“If I stop moving, something bad catches up with me. I don’t know what, exactly. So I stay busy, stay scrolling, stay planning, stay anywhere but here. Rest is supposed to feel good. For me it feels like a trap.”

Read more about flight

Fight

“I’m angry more than I want to be, at things that don’t deserve it. There’s a constant edge in me, like I’m ready for a confrontation that hasn’t been scheduled yet. People are starting to walk on eggshells around me, and I hate that.”

Read more about fight

Fawn

“I go along with what others want. Disagreeing doesn’t feel like an option, so I stay small, agreeable, and out of the way. Ask me what I want and you’ll get a pleasant answer that tells you nothing, because I stopped asking myself that a long time ago.”

Read more about fawn

Appease

“Others’ moods run my life. I manage their moods through the tone that I use, the timing, the topics I avoid. And I push my own values to the side to make sure others are okay. On the outside, I might be smiling, but internally, I’m constantly laboring.”

Read more about appease

Not sure

“Honestly? Some of these sound like me and some don’t, or it changes by the day, or none of it quite fits. I just know something’s off and I’m tired of guessing.”

Read more about not being sure
Go deeper

Go deeper into your state

Open any state to read what it is, why your body built it, and what tends to help. Open more than one if you’re comparing.

Shutdown

Shutdown is your nervous system’s deepest protective response. When your body concluded (at some point, for some good reason) that fighting wouldn’t help and running wasn’t possible, it did the last thing available: it powered down. The numbness, the heaviness, the distance from your own life, that’s conservation mode. Your body is spending as little as possible because it once needed to.

That means the flatness you feel isn’t a character flaw, and it isn’t proof you’ve stopped caring. The caring is still in there. It’s behind a protective layer your body built on purpose.

What tends to help is small and gentle. Not forcing motivation, not bullying yourself into action, but tiny doses of sensation and connection: warmth, a familiar voice, noticing one thing you can see or hear right now. Shutdown softens through safety, not effort.

And here’s the hopeful part: shutdown is a state, not a sentence. Bodies that learned to power down can learn, gradually, that it’s safe to power back up.

Freeze

Freeze is two things happening at once: your body is hitting the gas and the brake at the same time. Underneath your daily experience, there’s a huge amount of mobilized energy (that’s the racing mind, the inner scream), but clamped on top of it is an immobilizing brake.

Freeze is perhaps the most misunderstood stuck state. It gets confused with shutdown because both look immobile from the outside, but they feel completely different on the inside. Shutdown is collapsed immobility, disconnected and numb. Freeze is charged immobility, braced and tense. Knowing which one you’re in matters, because they need different things.

What tends to help with freeze is letting that trapped energy move in small, tolerable amounts: gentle movement, shaking out your hands, even slowly looking around the room. You’re not trying to force the brake off. You’re showing your body, a little at a time, that the gas pedal energy has somewhere safe to go. And of course, lots of safety state activation, which helps the freeze thaw over time.

There is real hope here. Think of it this way: all that energy locked inside you is capacity. It’s drive, momentum, and aliveness waiting for the brake to ease.

Flight

Flight is mobilized escape energy. Your nervous system fueled you up to get away from something, and that fuel is still in the tank: the restlessness, the racing thoughts, the busyness that never quite becomes peace. Anxiety is flight energy without a destination through the Polyvagal lens.

This made sense at some point. A body that learned the world has things worth escaping keeps the engine warm. That’s not weakness; that’s a system doing exactly what it was built to do, just longer than you need it to at this point.

What tends to help is giving the energy completion and direction rather than suppressing it. Movement that actually goes somewhere (a brisk walk counts), naming what you’re feeling so your body knows you’ve gotten the message, and practicing small moments of stillness that end before they become unbearable. You teach your body that the present moment is survivable, a few seconds at a time.

A reframe: flight energy is the same energy as motivation, productivity, creativity, and play... once it has somewhere to go and the safety state to carry it.

Fight

Fight is mobilized aggressive energy. Your nervous system armed you to protect something (yourself, someone you love, your dignity), and the weapons haven’t been put away. Fight shows up as the short fuse, the blaming, the arguments you win in the shower. Your body is holding a posture of readiness because, at some point, readiness was required.

So the anger isn’t evidence that you’re a bad or broken person. It’s protective energy with nowhere appropriate to land, and it tends to land on whoever’s nearby. You’ve probably noticed that, and you probably don’t like it. That noticing is worth something.

What tends to help is giving the energy a legitimate job: real physical exertion, firm boundaries spoken plainly, anything that lets your body complete the protective movement it’s been holding. Suppressing fight energy usually just stores it. Spending it on purpose, in ways you choose, is different. This becomes much easier as your safety state strengthens and can give your fight activation containment and a channel.

Some hope: fight energy matures into something valuable. It becomes the ability to say no, to stand your ground, to protect without exploding. The fire isn’t the problem. It just needs a fireplace.

Fawn

Fawn isn’t a separate nervous system state. It’s a behavioral adaptation built on top of significant freeze or shutdown. Somewhere along the way, your body learned that the safest move was to submit: stay small, stay agreeable, keep your head down. The going-along is the visible part; underneath it is a freeze or shutdown physiology doing the actual surviving.

First, plainly: if you’re doing this because someone in your life is actually unsafe, your nervous system is responding accurately, and you deserve real support beyond a webpage. Please reach out to someone who can help with the situation itself.

That’s why a useful early question for fawn is the freeze-versus-shutdown question: when you strip away the accommodating, is what’s underneath charged and tense, or collapsed and numb? (The freeze and shutdown sections above describe the difference.) Knowing what’s under the fawning tells you what your body actually needs.

What tends to help is small and private at first: noticing a preference (which mug, which route, which song) before ever needing to voice one, and spending time with people who don’t punish your no. Preferences come back the way feeling returns to a numb limb, gradually and with some tingling.

The hope: your attunement to others is real skill. Once it becomes a choice instead of a reflex, it’s one of your best qualities, not your cage.

Appease

Appease, like fawn, is arguably a behavioral adaptation rather than a true nervous system state of its own. It sits on top of significant freeze or shutdown. The difference: fawn hides and submits to stay safe; appease builds a fake connection to placate. Reading moods, choosing your words, timing your requests, keeping the temperature down. It’s skilled, exhausting, and largely invisible to everyone but you.

First, plainly: if you’re doing this because someone in your life is actually unsafe, your nervous system is responding accurately, and you deserve real support beyond a webpage. Please reach out to someone who can help with the situation itself.

If the danger has passed but the pattern remains, the same question that helps with fawn helps here: underneath all that managing, is your body in freeze (charged, braced) or shutdown (numb, collapsed)? The sections above describe the difference, and the answer points to your starting place.

The hope: all that vigilance was intelligence in service of survival. The same perceptiveness, pointed at your own needs, becomes self-knowledge.

Not sure

If nothing above gave you an obvious “Hey, that’s me,” you’re not doing this wrong. Many people struggle to identify their state, especially at first. The figuring-out isn’t a delay before the real thing starts. The figuring-out is part of the process.

A few honest possibilities: you might be in more than one state, you may have one dominant state that shows up in different ways, you may fluctuate between dominant states... These are all potentials and not uncommon.

If you skipped the checklist above, try it now; that’s exactly what it’s for.
